    Notes
    Layers

    Layers

    No boundary for any of these lands is set by revelation.

    The Qur'an names blessed places but never uses the words al-Shām, Filasṭīn or al-Ḥijāz. The Sunnah and the Companions use al-Shām and al-Ḥijāz as regions everyone already knew. The lines came later: from ʿUmar's military districts (ajnād), from jurists defining al-Ḥijāz for a single ruling, and from geographers who disagree at every edge.

    Only two places have a boundary the texts actually fix: the ḥarams of Makkah and Madinah, shown in detail below the map. On the map, solid colour marks land that every major source includes and hatching marks land that only some include.

    • Tier 1Revelation: the Qur'an and the authentic Sunnah
    • Tier 2Companions, Successors and early scholars (1st–3rd c. AH)
    • Tier 3Classical geographers (3rd–8th c. AH)
    • Tier 4Modern borders (20th century to today)

    Reading the map

    Lines and colour

    Solid: well established. Coasts and present-day borders.
    Dashed: approximate. The landmarks are known but the line between them is not, such as the ḥaram outlines and the old roads.
    Dotted: disputed or uncertain. The sources disagree, the edge moved over time, or I found no source for a line and drew only a rough indication.
    Solid colour: land that every major source includes in the region.
    Hatching: land that some sources include and others leave out. Where two regions' hatching crosses, the sources disagree about which region the land belongs to.

    The shaded relief shows mountains and escarpments; the sand stipple marks the great deserts; the faint grid is latitude and longitude.

    Badges and discs

    Lettered circles (A–P): places a source names as a limit of a region. Tap one to read the source's own words.
    Numbered discs (1–22): the sacred-status entries explained in the table below. A disc marks a place or a whole land, never an area; where it sits off its site, a thin line leads back.
    ḥaram muqaddas mubārak faḍīla link none established
    Qur'an or Sunnah the Salaf later scholars, or disputed with a “?”

    Use the View buttons above the map to switch between the overview, lands and boundaries, sacred status and the roads, or the layer list to switch single layers.

    Sacred status: what the evidence establishes 22 entries

    The numbers match the discs on the map; tap a number to find it there. Two questions are kept apart in every row: what gives the place its status, and what fixes where it is and how far it reaches. “Level” says which kind of source carries the claim.

Where the early commentators differ, the difference is about which land or how far, and each row says so.

    Four layers of evidence

    Each layer is kept separate. Where I connect them, it is marked as my synthesis. A dagger † marks a statement taken from the earlier atlas this one grew from and not re-checked against the sources.

    Tier 1

    Revelation

    The Qur'an and the authentic Sunnah. Boundaries set: none, except the two ḥarams.

    al-Shām

    • The word does not occur in the Qur'an. Its root appears only as al-mashʾamah, “the left” (56:9, 90:19).
    • “The land We blessed” (21:71, 21:81, 7:137, 34:18). Al-Baghawī explains 21:71 and 21:81 as al-Shām.
    • The Sunnah uses al-Shām as a known region: al-Juḥfah is the mīqāt for it (al-Bukhārī 1524), and a fire from the land of al-Ḥijāz will light the necks of the camels at Buṣrā (al-Bukhārī 7118). I found no authenticated hadith that defines its borders.

    Filasṭīn

    • The name does not occur in the Qur'an.
    • 17:1: al-Aqṣā, “whose surroundings We have blessed”: a blessing, not a boundary.
    • 5:21, “the holy land”: five answers in the early commentary (row 9).

    al-Ḥijāz

    • The word does not occur. Its root appears only as ḥājiz, “a barrier” (27:61, 69:47).
    • The Sunnah names “the land of al-Ḥijāz” (al-Bukhārī 7118) and commands the expulsion of the mushrikūn from Jazīrat al-ʿArab (al-Bukhārī 3053, Muslim 1637), a ruling that gave jurists a reason to define al-Ḥijāz.

    Neighbouring lands

    • Miṣr is named (12:99; also 10:87, 12:21, 43:51). In 2:61 the word is miṣran, which al-Ṭabarī reports Qatādah, al-Suddī, Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd reading as "any town", and he leaves the question open. Sabaʾ is named (34:15–19), and the Prophet ﷺ said Sabaʾ was a man with ten sons (al-Tirmidhī 3222). al-Aḥqāf (46:21) and al-Rūm (30:2–4) are named.
    • al-Ḥabashah is not in the Qur'an; it is in the Sunnah.
    • I found no verse or authentic hadith that calls Iraq a ḥaram, holy or blessed. The Sunnah gives it a mīqāt.
    Tier 2

    Companions and early scholars

    1st–3rd c. AH. Working divisions, not a fixed map.

    al-Shām

    • ʿUmar organised it into ajnād: Filasṭīn, al-Urdunn, Dimashq and Ḥimṣ. Qinnasrīn was split off later, under Muʿāwiyah or Yazīd, and al-ʿAwāṣim under Hārūn al-Rashīd.
    • At Sargh ʿUmar was met by “the commanders of the ajnād” (al-Bukhārī, Muslim), so the districts existed in the Companions' time.
    • Ibn Kathīr: ʿUmar counted Taymāʾ and Wādī al-Qurā as al-Shām (badge E). Al-Ṭabarī: all agree the Holy Land lies between the Euphrates and al-ʿArīsh (badge A).

    Filasṭīn

    • Early usage treats Filasṭīn as a named part inside al-Shām: Ibrāhīm settled at al-Sabʿ “of the land of Filasṭīn” (Ibn Isḥāq, badge M); Usāmah was sent to al-Dārūm (badge N).
    • On 30:3, Muqātil names “al-Urdunn and Filasṭīn” side by side (badge O).
    • Jund Filasṭīn's capital was Ludd, then al-Ramlah, founded around 715 CE.

    al-Ḥijāz

    • Physical sense: the mountain chain that “bars” low Tihāmah from high Najd (Hishām b. al-Kalbī); al-Aṣmaʿī: Makkah is Tihāmī, Madinah and al-Ṭāʾif are Ḥijāzī.
    • Legal sense: al-Shāfiʿī, Makkah, Madinah, al-Yamāmah and their districts; Aḥmad adds Khaybar, Yanbuʿ and Fadak † (badge J).
    • Outlier: al-Ḥarbī, “Tabūk and Filasṭīn are of al-Ḥijāz” (via Yāqūt). Not drawn.

    Neighbouring lands

    • On 30:3 Mujāhid takes “the nearest land” to be al-Jazīrah. On 46:21 three early reports place al-Aḥqāf at al-Shiḥr (Qatādah), Mahrah (Muqātil) or between ʿUmān and Mahrah (Ibn ʿAbbās).
    Tier 3

    Classical geographers

    3rd–8th c. AH. Explicit lines, but they differ.

    al-Shām

    • Ibn Ḥawqal (4th c.): the Sea of al-Rūm to the west; the desert “from Ayla to the Euphrates” to the east; the Euphrates up to the Byzantine frontier, taking in the frontier fortresses; Egypt to the south, ending at Rafaḥ.
    • Yāqūt (d. 626 AH): length from the Euphrates to al-ʿArīsh; width from the two mountains of Ṭayyiʾ to the sea (badges A, F). The widest line.
    • Abū al-Fidāʾ (d. 732 AH): a narrower settled-land line, roughly the solid core.
    • Al-Muqaddasī counts six districts, adding al-Sharāt †.

    Filasṭīn

    • The geographers list Filasṭīn as a district of al-Shām, the westernmost, from Rafaḥ to al-Lajjūn (badge K).
    • Disputed towns include Arīḥāʾ and ʿAmmān (badge L).
    • Nāṣir-i Khusraw notes that al-Ramlah itself was called “Filasṭīn” †. Under the Mamluks and Ottomans the unit broke into smaller districts, though the name stayed in use †.

    al-Ḥijāz

    • Yāqūt gathers the earlier definitions and records Sargh as “the first of al-Ḥijāz” (badge D).
    • Al-Qazwīnī: “a barrier between Yemen and al-Shām, a month's journey” †.
    • Result: a firm core (Makkah, al-Ṭāʾif, Madinah, Yanbuʿ, Khaybar, Fadak) with a soft north, south and east.

    Neighbouring lands

    • Al-Iṣṭakhrī gives al-Jazīrah, al-ʿIrāq and Miṣr chapters of their own. Yāqūt on Miṣr: from the two trees between Rafaḥ and al-ʿArīsh to Aswān, and from Barqah to Aylah.
    • Yāqūt on Tihāmah: it runs along the sea, and Makkah is of it.
    Synthesis (mine)The seam between al-Shām and al-Ḥijāz is a band, not a line. ʿUmar, per al-Balādhurī, put it at Wādī al-Qurā; the geographers' “first of al-Ḥijāz, last of al-Shām” sits at Sargh, north of Tabūk. The two are a few hundred kilometres apart, and both are defensible readings of their own time. The map shows them overlapping rather than choosing.
    Tier 4

    Modern political borders

    20th century to today. Surveyed lines, drawn for other reasons.

    al-Shām

    • After 1918 the British and French mandates divided it into Syria, Lebanon, Palestine and Transjordan; Hatay joined Türkiye in 1939 †.
    • None of these borders follows an old jund line.

    Filasṭīn

    • The Mandate border is not Jund Filasṭīn. It added Galilee, Acre, Haifa, Tiberias and Baysān, all old al-Urdunn, and the Negev to Eilat; it left out the east-bank lands that some sources gave Filasṭīn †.

    al-Ḥijāz

    • Now mainly Saudi Arabia's Makkah and Madinah provinces and part of the Tabūk region.
    • Maʿān and ʿAqaba belonged to the Hashemite Kingdom of the Ḥijāz until 1925, when Britain attached them to Transjordan †.

    Neighbouring lands

    • Al-Jazīrah is split between Syria, Türkiye and Iraq; al-Ḥabashah lies in Ethiopia and Eritrea; Tihāmah is split between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

    The map uses Natural Earth's de facto lines. They are not an endorsement of any claim; see the honest limits below.

    Four different words

    Ḥaramحَرَم
    A sanctuary in which Allah ﷻ forbade hunting and cutting the vegetation. Makkah is a ḥaram by the agreement of the Muslims, and Madinah by the view of most scholars (the Ḥanafī school is reported to differ; not re-checked). Whether Wajj near al-Ṭāʾif is a third is disputed, and its hadith is graded weak by al-Albānī.
    Muqaddasمُقَدَّس
    Holy or purified. The Qur'an uses it for al-arḍ al-muqaddasah (al-Māʾidah 5:21) and the valley of Ṭuwā (Ṭā Hā 20:12; al-Nāziʿāt 79:16), where al-Baghawī glosses it “purified”. The same Arabic is rendered “blessed valley” in 20:12 and “sacred valley” in 79:16 by Saheeh International. The map does not treat these lands as a ḥaram; whether special rulings attach to them is a question for the scholars.
    Mubārakمُبَارَك
    Blessed. Used for the House at Bakkah (3:96), the surroundings of al-Aqṣā (17:1), the land of 7:137, 21:71 and 21:81, the villages of 34:18, and the spot where Mūsā عليه السلام was called (28:30); in the Sunnah, for Wādī al-ʿAqīq (al-Bukhārī 1534). Al-Baghawī explains the blessing in several of these as water, trees, fruit and abundance.
    Faḍīlaفَضِيلَة
    A stated virtue, “best”. The Prophet ﷺ said of Makkah that it is the best of the land of Allah ﷻ (al-Tirmidhī 3925, which al-Tirmidhī calls ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ gharīb; also Ibn Mājah 3108, ṣaḥīḥ in the Darussalam grading on sunnah.com), and the Sunnah gives virtues to Madinah, Qubāʾ, Uḥud and others. Scholars are reported to differ on whether Makkah or Madinah is better; I did not re-check each school's position.

    Where the classical lands sit today

    “Core” means inside the solid colour on the map; “edges” means the hatched or dotted zones. The first four rows come from the earlier atlas †; the rows marked “my mapping” follow my own outlines on the map and carry only the certainty those outlines have.

This one is Upper Mesopotamia.

I could not re-read the geographers' formula for its limits.Modern Iraq's borders also take in al-Jazīrah in the north (Mosul) and the western desert, which the old lists put elsewhere.

    TihāmahThe Red Sea coastal plain of Saudi Arabia and Yemen, including Makkah and Jeddah in the strict sense.The northern end near Yanbuʿ is my guess.Often confused with al-Ḥijāz; they overlap on the map.

    Reading these maps honestly

    The lines are my reconstruction

    Classical authors describe limits by naming towns, deserts and rivers. I placed the lines from those descriptions, from the real courses of rivers and coasts, and from modern studies. Treat every edge as rough, tens of kilometres at best, and the dotted edges as ranges, not lines.

    The districts moved over time

    The ajnād of 640 CE, 900 CE and 1050 CE were not identical; the borders drawn here are schematic.

    Discs mark places, not areas

    A numbered disc stands for a place or a whole land, not for its extent. Some discs are moved off their site, with a thin line leading back, so the labels stay readable. Where the sources give no edge (al-Aqṣā's surroundings, the Holy Land, “the land We blessed”), the map uses a dashed or dotted ring, never a line.

    Even the two ḥaram lines are drawn by hand

    In the Makkah detail map the points are the boundary sites al-Nawawī names, placed at approximate positions, with the curve between them interpolated. Madinah's outline joins the landmarks the hadith names and is looser still. The Sinai marker is the traditional Jabal Mūsā, not an identification the Qur'an makes. The enclosure of al-Aqṣā is a small hand-drawn shape.

    The new neighbouring lands

    The river-bounded shapes (al-Jazīrah, the Sawād, the Nile valley and Delta) follow real river courses; the edges that rest on towns or distances, with no source I could read, are dotted. Najd, al-Baḥrayn and Tihāmah are rough indications only. The sizes of the three al-Aḥqāf rings are illustrative.

    Modern borders come from Natural Earth

    They are public-domain de facto lines. They do not show recent changes on the ground, and several are disputed: Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, the Golan Heights, Shebaa and Ḥalāʾib are drawn as hatched disputed areas. The earlier atlas makes claims about which states recognise the Golan annexation and about the buffer zone since December 2024; I could not check them, so I left them out.

    What I could not verify

    • The geographers' formulas for the limits of al-ʿIrāq (Tikrīt to ʿAbbādān and the like), al-Jazīrah, Najd, al-Yamāmah and al-Baḥrayn. I tried again and the pages I could reach gave summaries, not the original text, so I added no limit I could not read myself.
    • The Ḥijāz lists attributed to al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad, and the Ḥanafī position on Madinah's ḥaram.
    • The shape of al-Ḥabashah beyond Aksūm.
    • The Golan recognition claims.

    A caliphate outline a thought experiment · not a ruling

    Two outlines, kept apart. The first is mine: the smallest single territory holding every land the sources give a status. The second is the author’s specification: a much wider area. No text, early scholar or geographer drew either one. The texts on the caliphate are in the first column.

    From revelation

    What the texts say

    Qur'an 24:55. لَيَسْتَخْلِفَنَّهُمْ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ "Allāh ﷻ has promised those who have believed among you and done righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession [to authority] upon the earth just as He granted it to those before them…" (Saheeh International). Al-Baghawī reports from Abū al-ʿĀliyah that it came down when the Companions lived in fear, and says the verse points to the caliphate of Abū Bakr and the imamate of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. Ibn Kathīr describes the promise as fulfilled in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime and under Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿUthmān.

    Thirty years, then kingship. "Al-Khilafah will be in my Ummah for thirty years, then there will be monarchy after that" (al-Tirmidhī 2226, from Safīnah; graded ḥasan).

    A return foretold. A hadith in Musnad Aḥmad (18406), told by al-Nuʿmān b. Bashīr from Ḥudhayfah b. al-Yamān, lists prophethood, then a caliphate on the method of prophethood, then biting kingship, then tyrannical kingship, "then there will be a caliphate on the method of prophethood", after which the Prophet ﷺ fell silent (my rendering of the Arabic). Al-Albānī graded its chain ḥasan.

    A warning sign. "Ibn Hawalah, when you see the caliphate has settled in the holy land, earthquakes, sorrows and serious matters will have drawn near" (Abū Dāwūd 2535; ṣaḥīḥ according to al-Albānī).

    None of these texts gives the caliphate a border.

    My synthesis

    The best-lands outline

    It is the smallest single territory that holds every land the sources give a status: al-Ḥijāz with the two ḥarams (entries 1–7), al-Shām with Filasṭīn and al-Aqṣā (8–11), Sinai and al-Ṭūr (12), al-Yaman (14) and Miṣr (15). Where the sources disagree on an edge, I took the widest reading, so every hatched zone of al-Shām and al-Ḥijāz is inside. For Miṣr I took only the Nile valley and the Delta, not Yāqūt's desert rectangle. Tihāmah joins al-Ḥijāz to al-Yaman.

    What falls outside is telling. Najd, al-ʿIrāq, the Gulf coast, al-Ḥabashah and Bilād al-Rūm have no established status (entries 16, 20 and 21), so they are not in it. The table still shows a tenth of Iraq: its western desert, which falls inside only because al-Shām's widest reading reaches the Euphrates. The best lands form a ring around the Red Sea and up the Levant.

    Present-day states and territories inside the outline. Areas are my rough measurement from these outlines.
    State or territoryArea inside, km²Share of it
    The author’s specification

    The core caliphate: Dār al-Amān

    Drawn to the author’s specification. It is not from the sources, and not a ruling. The core caliphate is named Dār al-Amān (دار الأمان), with the formal title al-Khilāfa al-Amīna (الخلافة الأمينة), its people Amānī (plural Amāniyyūn) and al-Quds (Jerusalem) as its capital. None of these names comes from the sources. The lands the sources honour are inside the black dotted line; everything between that line and the core caliphate comes from the specification.

    The versions, from the smallest to the largest. V1 is the sixteen states of a Middle East reference map, whole: Türkiye, Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, Jordan, Iraq, Iran, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Yemen, with the whole of Libya and the lands of the whole Nile (Sudan, South Sudan, Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi) added; the best-lands outline lies inside it. V2 holds the best-lands outline with the whole Arabian Peninsula, Greater Syria, Greater Israel in its widest reading, all of Iraq and Iran (with Greater Iraq), Türkiye, the South Caucasus, Cyprus, Egypt, Sudan, South Sudan and the Horn of Africa, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi (so the whole Nile and Lake Victoria are inside), Libya, Tunisia, Greece, and Turkmenistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan, whole, with all of Greater Khurāsān (about 1.16 million km², to the Oxus); it ends at Tunisia’s western border. V3 is V5 stopping at Iraq’s eastern border. V4 is V1 with Morocco, Western Sahara, Algeria, Tunisia, Afghanistan and Pakistan, each whole. V5 adds to V2 the rest of North Africa (Algeria, Morocco, Western Sahara and Mauritania), Transoxiana (all of Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan), Spain and Portugal, Sicily and Malta, Derbent and the Dagestan coast, the island of Arwād; V3, V6 and V7 are built on it. V5 thus holds every land of a Greater Middle East reference map. V6 adds to V5 Corsica and Sardinia, the Muslim-majority countries of Africa, Cameroon, and East Turkestan (Xinjiang, with a strip of western Gansu), and sets out how Muslim rulers held each land. V7 adds to V5 the Muslim-majority countries of Africa, the ruled part of every land a caliphate once ruled, and the lands that join them up. Two overlays can be drawn over any version: the Natural line, one ring of natural features (rivers, crests, watersheds, escarpments and coasts) round the complete outline, and the Internal lines (the Taurus divide, the Nile, Tigris and Euphrates, and the Red Sea as the axis).

    Each version’s note on the map gives its lands, the history of each, and how it was drawn. The names, the natural ring and the rule for the joined lands are the author’s design; the edges of the historical lands are approximate.

    VersionLines

    What the sources say about the added lands. The atlas finds no established sacred status for them, Iraq included (entries 16, 20 and 21). For Cyprus, Persia, Khurāsān and the lands of the west, Ibn Kathīr, on 24:55, records conquest under ʿUmar and ʿUthmān; for Türkiye, the old Bilād al-Rūm, the hadith praise an army that campaigns against Caesar's city, not the land (entry 21). That is conquest history, not a status. For al-Ḥabashah the Sunnah says the opposite of a claim: دَعُوا الْحَبَشَةَ مَا وَدَعُوكُمْ "Let the Abyssinians alone as long as they let you alone" (Abū Dāwūd 4302; ḥasan according to al-Albānī).

    Precedent and limits

    What it would mean

    It has existed before. Ibn Kathīr, on 24:55, describes Abū Bakr taking control of the whole Arabian Peninsula, and ʿUmar's reign adding the rest of al-Shām, Egypt and most of Persia. By the end of ʿUmar's caliphate, most of the lands in the best-lands outline were under one rule, inside a much larger state. This part is my own summary of general history, not checked against a source in this atlas: the outline uses the widest reading of al-Shām, and its frontier fortresses (Ṭarsūs, Marʿash, Malaṭyah) were probably not yet securely held. Much of the wider outline, including al-Ḥabashah, was not under that rule either.

    Today the best-lands outline would cross ten states and territories, and the core caliphate twenty-five, among them Israel, the state that serves the two ḥarams, and countries where most people are not Muslim. The only road to such a union without war is the free consent of the people who live there. In 2014, 126 scholars wrote to the leader of ISIS, who had declared a caliphate by force: "It is forbidden in Islam to declare a caliphate without consensus from all Muslims."

    Muslims disagree about the caliphate today. Some hold that restoring it is an obligation. Others hold that its aims, such as justice and the protection of religion and life, can be served by cooperating states. Many read the hadith of a returning caliphate as news of what Allah ﷻ will bring about, not as a plan for any group to carry out. This page does not settle that question; ask qualified scholars.

    My reading, not a ruling: the texts describe what will happen and tie a caliphate in the Holy Land to upheaval. They do not draw a border to fight for.

    Regional index the core caliphate and V7

    Twenty-seven regions, named as the classical geographers and chroniclers named them (the joined lands have no classical name here and are named plainly), with the present-day states in each. Seventeen make up the core caliphate (V5). V7 takes in all of them, adds three for the Muslim-majority countries of Africa, adds nine that caliphates once ruled, counting only the part that was ruled, and adds three more, joined to the rest. Tap a region to see it on the map. Areas are my rough measurement; classical names are approximate guides, not borders.

    Sources

    Texts

    • Qur'an text, the Saheeh International translation, and the tafsir of al-Baghawī (with al-Ṭabarī on 5:21 and Ibn Kathīr on 24:55), retrieved from quran.com through quran.ai. Where the page quotes an English rendering it is Saheeh International's own wording. English names for lands (for example "the Holy Land" for al-arḍ al-muqaddasah) are this atlas's own: Saheeh International renders 5:21 "the blessed land [i.e., Palestine]", and the bracket is the translators' gloss, not the Arabic.
    • Hadith references and gradings checked on sunnah.com; the Madinah ḥaram hadith on dorar.net.
    • Al-Nawawī on the Makkah ḥaram limits (Islamweb fatwa 71668); Ibn Taymiyyah on the ḥarams.
    • Yāqūt, Muʿjam al-Buldān: s.v. Miṣr, Tihāmah, al-Ḥijāz.
    • Al-Iṣṭakhrī, al-Masālik wa-l-Mamālik, on Miṣr, al-Jazīrah and al-ʿIrāq (al-Shāmilah).
    • Ibn Ḥawqal and Abū al-Fidāʾ on al-Shām, quoted in al-Muqtabas no. 70.
    • Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāyah wa-l-Nihāyah, on Taymāʾ and Wādī al-Qurā (Wikisource); the earlier atlas linked a text it gave as al-Balādhurī’s, not re-checked.

    Geography

    • Base map: Natural Earth 1:10m countries, disputed areas, lakes and rivers, and shaded relief (public domain). The Nile, Euphrates and Tigris shapes are traced from Natural Earth's river lines.
    • Saudipedia: the mīqāts; historical Hajj routes.
    • Darb Zubaydah; Jund Filasṭīn; Bilād al-Shām.
    • Sargh and the Syrian Hajj road (al-Saḥrāʾ).
    • Lands once ruled by caliphates (V7’s historical additions): Córdoba, the Almohads, Septimania, Fraxinetum, Sicily, Bari, Malta, Crete, Ottoman territorial changes, Ottoman Hungary, Uyvar, Ragusa, the Crimean Khanate, Podolia, Derbent, Sokoto, Adamawa, Tibesti, Equatoria, the caliphate in India, Iltutmish, al-Qādir and the Karakhanids, Yettishar. Province boundaries for the ruled parts: Natural Earth admin-1 states and provinces.
    • Muslim-majority countries of Africa (V7’s African additions): Pew Research Center, religious composition table, 2010 and 2020 (appendix B, June 2025); Pew on Nigeria; Islam in Nigeria, Religion in Guinea-Bissau, Chad and Burkina Faso (census and survey figures). The figures were read through a page-summarising tool and not checked cell by cell in the PDF.
